messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan stepped out of his truck at the trailhead and felt the familiar knot tighten in his chest. A group of hikers was gathered near the map kiosk, and one of them—a man in his fifties with a worn green cap—was telling a story about his time in the army. The words “deployment” and “convoy” drifted through the morning air, and Rohan’s jaw clenched. He turned abruptly and walked toward the maintenance shed, the only place on this section of the preserve where he knew he would be alone. He told himself he needed to check the chainsaw fuel, but the real reason was simpler: he could not bear to be within earshot of any military talk.

Three years earlier, Rohan had been part of a small conservation team working in a remote region of Southeast Asia. They had been taken by a militia group that wore mismatched fatigues and carried automatic weapons. For six weeks, Rohan was kept in a concrete room with no windows. He was beaten across his ribs and the backs of his legs whenever he failed to answer a question correctly—the questions changed each time, so he never knew what the right answer was. The worst part was the unpredictability: one guard would bring him water, the next would kick him in the same spot. He learned to watch for the smallest change in a person’s posture or tone, because that flicker of movement meant something was about to happen.

Now, back home and working as a park ranger in a quiet state forest, Rohan’s body still reacted as if the danger had never stopped. An unexpected movement in his peripheral vision—a deer jumping across the trail, a child darting behind a picnic table—would send a jolt through his whole frame, his hands flying up before his mind could catch up. When a ranger from another district drove by in a patrol vehicle, the sight of the uniform made his stomach drop. He knew intellectually that this man was a colleague, not a captor, but that knowledge never reached the part of him that still existed inside that concrete room.

The memory itself came in fragments. He could recall the guard’s boots, the crack in the ceiling, the sound of a generator starting—each moment a frozen snapshot, isolated from the others. Sometimes, when the memory surfaced, he felt a sharp pain in his ribs and the backs of his legs, as if the bruises were fresh. Other times, he could describe the entire six weeks to his girlfriend, Sarah, in a flat, detached voice, feeling nothing at all, as though he were narrating someone else’s life. That numbness frightened him more than the pain.

To manage the constant sense of impending threat, Rohan had developed a strict set of invisible rules. He controlled his eating with military precision: exactly two meals a day, the same portion size, no snacks. If he lost control of that, he reasoned, everything else would follow. When he was around other people—fellow rangers, hikers, even Sarah—he said yes to whatever they wanted, agreed with whatever plan they proposed, because disagreeing had once meant punishment. He kept his head down and his voice soft. But alone in his truck, or lying awake at three in the morning, he allowed himself the full, bitter pleasure of revenge fantasies. He imagined the faces of the three men who had interrogated him; he imagined what he would do to them if the roles were reversed. The fantasy gave him a feeling of power that he never felt in his actual life.

Those fantasies were the only time he did not feel isolated. At work, he watched his colleagues joke and trade stories around the lunch table, and he knew he could never join them. He was certain they would look at him differently if they knew what had happened. Worse, he believed that someone stronger, someone smarter, would never have been taken in the first place. He had walked into that situation, after all—he had accepted the assignment—so the humiliation was his to carry.

The moment that finally pushed him to seek help came on a Tuesday afternoon. He was clearing a fallen branch from a trail when a mountain biker rounded a bend too fast, nearly colliding with him. Rohan dropped the branch, threw himself sideways into a bush, and let out a yell that startled both of them. The biker apologized profusely, but Rohan could not stop shaking. He sat on the ground for ten minutes, his ribs aching from no blow. That evening, he told Sarah he needed to talk to someone. He did not know if talking would help—he had never believed that safety was possible, no matter what anyone said—but he was tired of living inside the snapshots.
